summary: Teach body temperature regulation (ages 12–14) as a negative-feedback control loop: the body detects a deviation from ~37°C, triggers responses that OPPOSE the change, and restores the set point. Learners should name two cooling mechanisms (sweating, vasodilation) and two warming mechanisms (shivering, vasoconstriction), explain the mechanism of each (e.g. sweat cools by evaporation, not wetness), and link a stable core temperature to enzymes working best near 37°C and denaturing if too hot (while cold slows enzymes rather than denaturing them). A dynamic feedback model is the primary vehicle; a labelled skin cross-section and a categorisation/sequencing task support the naming and loop-ordering layers; a brief predictive discussion and a hands-on evaporation test anchor the mechanism.
misconceptions: Thinking blood vessels physically move toward or away from the skin surface (they widen/narrow in place — vasodilation/vasoconstriction).
Believing sweat cools you just by being wet, rather than by EVAPORATING and taking heat away.
Thinking responses add to the change rather than oppose it (missing negative feedback).
Assuming shivering is involuntary trembling with no purpose, rather than muscle activity releasing heat.
Thinking body temperature simply matches the environment rather than being actively regulated.

activities.title: Hold the body at 37°C: a negative-feedback model
steps: Change a simulated environment to blazing heat or biting cold and watch a core-temperature dial begin to drift away from 37°C.

Observe and name the responses that fire: in heat, skin vessels widen (skin reddens, more blood near the surface) and sweat appears and evaporates, so the dial eases back down; in cold, vessels narrow, shivering begins, and the dial climbs back up.

Follow a feedback-loop diagram that lights stage by stage — stimulus → detect (receptors in skin and brain) → control centre in the brain (hypothalamus) processes and signals → respond (effectors) → return to set point — and state in your own words how each response OPPOSES the original change.

Use a 'switch off responses' control: with feedback disabled in a HOT environment, watch core temperature overshoot 37°C until an enzyme-denaturing warning appears; in a COLD environment the dial instead falls below 37°C and enzymes slow down rather than denature. Either way, explain why the loop matters.
Predict before each manipulation what the body should do, then check against the model.
activities.insight: Thermoregulation is a self-correcting control loop, not just a list of reactions: the body senses a deviation and acts to reverse it (negative feedback), and a constant ~37°C is needed so enzymes keep working — overheating denatures them, while severe cold slows them.

activities.title: Label the skin and bust the 'wet = cool' myth
steps: Explore a labelled skin cross-section (sweat glands, blood vessels near the surface, hair erector muscles) and attach each structure to a cooling or warming role, noting that hair erector muscles (goosebumps) trap an insulating air layer in furry animals but have very little warming effect in humans.
Explain for each: sweat evaporates and takes heat away; surface blood vessels widen to lose heat (vasodilation) or narrow to keep it (vasoconstriction).
Answer a reveal prompt — 'Do blood vessels move to the surface?' — then check the correction: 'No — vessels near the skin widen or narrow; they don't migrate.'
State why sweat cools far less on a humid day than a dry one.
activities.insight: Names the structures and responses accurately and understands that sweat cools by evaporation (change of state removing heat), not by being wet or cold, and that vasodilation/vasoconstriction is widening/narrowing rather than vessel movement.

activities.title: Sort and sequence the feedback loop
steps: Categorise responses into cooling (sweating, vasodilation) versus warming (shivering, vasoconstriction).
Put the negative-feedback stages in order: stimulus → detect/receptor → control centre (brain/hypothalamus) → respond/effector → return to set point.
Answer why maintaining ~37°C matters, linking it to enzyme activity and denaturation when too hot.
Justify each sort by stating how that response moves heat.
activities.insight: Consolidates the cooling/warming distinction, the ordering of the feedback loop, and the enzyme rationale for a constant core temperature.

activities.title: Predict-then-discuss: why do you sweat and shiver?
steps: Before using the model, predict out loud: what happens when you're too hot, and what happens when you're too cold?
Explain why you think you shiver, and what shivering does.
Compare your prediction with what the model shows and revise your reasoning aloud.
activities.insight: Surfaces prior ideas (including the 'warm-blooded means always warm automatically' and 'shivering is purposeless' beliefs) so they can be tested and refined against the model.

activities.title: Evaporative cooling hands-on test
steps: Put a drop of room-temperature or lukewarm water (or a dab from an alcohol wipe) on the back of one hand and leave the other dry.
Predict which hand will feel cooler and WHY before fanning both hands.
Fan both hands to speed evaporation and feel the difference.
Explain the result in terms of evaporation removing heat, and predict what would happen in humid air.
activities.insight: Experiences directly that cooling comes from evaporation (change of state taking heat from the skin), not from the water being cold or wet — and that reduced evaporation (humid air) means less cooling.

checkQuestion: On a hot day you sweat. How does sweating actually cool you down — what is it about the sweat that lowers your temperature? Explain.
checkAnswer: Sweat cools you as it EVAPORATES: turning from liquid to vapour takes energy (heat) from your skin, so the skin loses heat and cools; it isn't the wetness itself but the evaporation that does the cooling — which is why sweat cools you far less in humid air.
